lessons.title: Programming Fundamentals
lessons.summary_md: Every language shares the same building blocks: **values and variables**, **conditionals and loops**, and **functions** that turn inputs into outputs. Learn to read an error message, add a print/log statement, and step through code in a debugger before moving on.
key_points: Variables hold values; types decide what operations are valid
Loops and conditionals control which code runs
Functions take inputs and return outputs; keep them small
Debug by reproducing, isolating and checking one assumption at a time

lessons.title: Command Line Basics
lessons.summary_md: The terminal is where developer tools live. Learn to move around (`cd`, `ls`, `pwd`), inspect files (`cat`, `less`, `grep`), and combine commands with pipes (`|`) and redirection (`>`). Environment variables and `PATH` explain why a command is or is not found.
key_points: Paths can be absolute or relative to the working directory
Pipes send one command's output into another
Environment variables configure programs; PATH lists where executables are searched
Exit code 0 means success

lessons.title: Git & Version Control
lessons.summary_md: Git records snapshots of your project as **commits**. Work happens on **branches**, which are merged back after review in a **pull request**. Know the everyday loop (`status`, `add`, `commit`, `pull`, `push`), how to resolve a merge conflict, and why you never rewrite shared history.
key_points: A commit is a snapshot plus a message explaining why
Branches isolate work; merges or rebases bring it back
Merge conflicts are resolved by editing the file and committing
Pull requests are where code review happens

lessons.title: How the Web Works (HTTP)
lessons.summary_md: A browser sends an **HTTP request** (method, URL, headers, optional body) and a server returns a **response** (status code, headers, body). GET reads, POST creates, PUT/PATCH update, DELETE removes. Status classes tell you what happened: 2xx success, 3xx redirect, 4xx client error, 5xx server error.
key_points: HTTP is stateless; cookies and tokens carry identity between requests
Methods describe intent; GET must not change data
4xx means the client sent something wrong, 5xx means the server failed
HTTPS adds TLS encryption on top of HTTP

lessons.title: Data Structures & Algorithms
lessons.summary_md: Most interview problems reduce to a handful of patterns: **hash maps** for lookups, **two pointers / sliding window** on arrays, **BFS/DFS** on trees and graphs, **heaps** for top-k, and **dynamic programming** for overlapping subproblems. Always state the time and space complexity in Big-O.
key_points: Hash maps give O(1) average lookups
Sorting is O(n log n); many problems get easier after sorting
BFS finds shortest paths in unweighted graphs
Dynamic programming caches answers to repeated subproblems

lessons.title: Software Testing
lessons.summary_md: Tests let you change code without fear. **Unit tests** check one function in isolation, **integration tests** check pieces working together, and **end-to-end tests** drive the real app. Follow Arrange-Act-Assert, keep tests deterministic, and mock only what you do not own.
key_points: The testing pyramid: many unit tests, fewer integration, few end-to-end
Arrange, Act, Assert
Flaky tests usually depend on time, order or the network
TDD: write a failing test, make it pass, refactor

lessons.title: System Design
lessons.summary_md: System design interviews test structured trade-off thinking. Clarify requirements and scale, sketch the **API and data model**, then add **load balancers, caches, replicas, shards and queues** only where the numbers demand them. Name the trade-offs explicitly: consistency vs availability, latency vs cost.
key_points: Start from requirements and back-of-the-envelope numbers
Scale reads with caches and replicas, writes with sharding and queues
CAP: under a partition you choose consistency or availability
Every component you add is a new failure mode

lessons.title: Web Security (OWASP)
lessons.summary_md: Most breaches exploit a short list of mistakes. **Injection** (SQL, command) is prevented with parameterised queries; **XSS** with output encoding and a Content Security Policy; **CSRF** with SameSite cookies or tokens. Never trust client input, store passwords with a slow hash, and keep secrets out of the repo.
key_points: Parameterised queries stop SQL injection
Escape output and use CSP against XSS
CORS controls which origins may read responses; it is not authentication
Hash passwords with bcrypt/argon2, never plain SHA

lessons.title: Behavioral Interviews (STAR)
lessons.summary_md: Behavioral answers follow **STAR**: Situation, Task, Action, Result. Prepare 6-8 stories that cover impact, conflict, failure, ambiguity and leadership, and quantify results. Spend most of the answer on **your** actions, not the team's.
key_points: Situation and Task set context in two sentences
Action is the longest part and uses "I"
Results are measurable and include what you learned
Reuse stories across questions by changing emphasis

lessons.title: HTML5 & Semantic Markup
lessons.summary_md: HTML describes **what content is**, not how it looks. Use semantic elements (`header`, `nav`, `main`, `article`, `button`) so browsers, search engines and screen readers understand the page. Forms need labels tied to inputs, and every image needs meaningful `alt` text.
key_points: Choose elements by meaning: a clickable action is a button
Every form input needs a label
Headings form an outline; do not skip levels
Meta tags control title, description and viewport

lessons.title: CSS Fundamentals
lessons.summary_md: CSS applies styles through the **cascade**: when rules conflict, the more **specific** selector wins, and later rules beat earlier ones of equal specificity. Every element is a **box** (content, padding, border, margin). Prefer relative units (`rem`, `%`) and set `box-sizing: border-box`.
key_points: Specificity: inline > id > class/attribute > element
The box model: content, padding, border, margin
rem scales with the root font size
Custom properties (variables) make themes easy

lessons.title: Flexbox & Grid Layout
lessons.summary_md: **Flexbox** lays items out along one axis: `justify-content` aligns on the main axis and `align-items` on the cross axis. **Grid** handles rows and columns together with `grid-template-columns` and `gap`. Use Flexbox for components, Grid for page layout.
key_points: Flexbox is one-dimensional, Grid is two-dimensional
justify-content = main axis, align-items = cross axis
fr units share leftover space in Grid
gap replaces margin hacks between items

lessons.title: Responsive Design
lessons.summary_md: Design **mobile-first**: write base styles for small screens, then add `min-width` media queries as space grows. Use fluid units, flexible images (`max-width: 100%`), and the viewport meta tag. Test at real breakpoints and with zoom.
key_points: Start with the smallest screen and enhance upward
min-width media queries pair with mobile-first
clamp() creates fluid type and spacing
Always include the viewport meta tag

lessons.title: Web Accessibility (WCAG)
lessons.summary_md: Accessible products work for everyone. Meet **WCAG AA**: text contrast of at least 4.5:1, every action reachable by **keyboard** with a visible focus ring, and semantic HTML before ARIA. Modals must trap focus and return it when closed.
key_points: Native elements beat ARIA roles
Contrast 4.5:1 for body text, 3:1 for large text
Everything clickable must be keyboard operable
Announce dynamic changes with live regions

lessons.title: JavaScript Fundamentals
lessons.summary_md: JavaScript runs in every browser and on servers via Node.js. Master `let`/`const` and **block scope**, **closures** (functions remember the scope they were created in), objects and **prototypes**, and array methods (`map`, `filter`, `reduce`). Use `===` to avoid type coercion surprises.
key_points: const prevents reassignment, not mutation
A closure keeps access to variables from its outer scope
map/filter/reduce return new arrays
=== compares without type coercion

lessons.title: DOM & Browser APIs
lessons.summary_md: The **DOM** is the live tree of the page. Select nodes with `querySelector`, update them, and listen with `addEventListener`. Events **bubble** from the target up to the document, which enables **event delegation**: one listener on a parent handles many children.
key_points: Events capture down, then bubble up
Event delegation uses one parent listener
Batch DOM writes to avoid layout thrashing
localStorage is synchronous and string-only

lessons.title: Async JavaScript & the Event Loop
lessons.summary_md: JavaScript is single-threaded; the **event loop** runs one task at a time. After each task it drains the **microtask queue** (promise callbacks) before the next macrotask (timers, I/O). `async/await` is syntax over promises: wrap awaits in `try/catch`, and use `Promise.all` to run independent work in parallel.
key_points: Microtasks (promises) run before the next macrotask (setTimeout)
await pauses only the current async function
Promise.all fails fast; Promise.allSettled waits for all
AbortController cancels fetches

lessons.title: TypeScript
lessons.summary_md: TypeScript adds a **static type checker** to JavaScript. Describe shapes with `interface`/`type`, model alternatives with **union types**, and let **narrowing** (`typeof`, `in`, discriminant fields) refine them. **Generics** keep functions reusable without losing types. Avoid `any`; prefer `unknown` at boundaries.
key_points: Types are erased at runtime; validate external data separately
Union + discriminant field = safe narrowing
Generics preserve the relationship between input and output types
unknown forces a check before use; any disables checking

lessons.title: React
lessons.summary_md: React builds UIs from **components**: functions that take **props** and return JSX. **State** (`useState`) triggers a re-render when it changes; **effects** (`useEffect`) sync with things outside React. Lists need stable `key`s, and derived values should be computed, not stored in state.
key_points: UI is a function of state
Props flow down; events flow up via callbacks
Keys must be stable and unique among siblings
Effects are for syncing with external systems, not for derived data

lessons.title: React State Management
lessons.summary_md: Keep state as **local** as possible and lift it only when siblings need it. Use **context** for rarely-changing global values (theme, user), a **store** (Redux Toolkit, Zustand) for complex client state, and a **server-state cache** (TanStack Query) for data fetched from APIs.
key_points: Server state and client state are different problems
Context re-renders every consumer on change
Stores allow selecting slices to limit re-renders
Normalise collections by id

lessons.title: Next.js & Server Rendering
lessons.summary_md: Next.js adds file-based **routing** and multiple rendering strategies to React. **Server Components** render on the server and send no JavaScript; **Client Components** (`"use client"`) handle interactivity. Choose static generation for content that rarely changes and server rendering for per-request data.
key_points: Server Components cannot use state or effects
Hydration attaches event handlers to server HTML
Static pages are fastest; revalidate to refresh them
Keep secrets in server-only code

lessons.title: Tailwind CSS
lessons.summary_md: Tailwind styles elements with small **utility classes** (`flex`, `p-4`, `text-sm`) mapped to a design-token scale. Responsive and state variants (`md:`, `hover:`) replace media queries and pseudo-classes. Extract repeated patterns into components, not long `@apply` blocks.
key_points: Utilities map to a consistent spacing/colour scale
Variants: md:, hover:, focus:, dark:
Configure tokens in the theme rather than hard-coding values
Unused classes are purged at build time

lessons.title: Build Tools & Bundlers
lessons.summary_md: Bundlers like **Vite** and **webpack** turn many modules into optimised files for the browser. They transpile TypeScript/JSX, **tree-shake** unused exports and **split** code into chunks. `package.json` declares dependencies; lockfiles pin exact versions for reproducible installs.
key_points: ES modules enable tree-shaking
Dynamic import() creates a separate chunk
Lockfiles make installs reproducible
Dev servers use hot module replacement

lessons.title: Frontend Testing
lessons.summary_md: Test components the way users use them: query by **role and label**, fire real events, and assert on what is visible. Use **Playwright** or Cypress for a few critical end-to-end flows. Avoid testing implementation details like internal state.
key_points: getByRole is the preferred query
Wait for UI with findBy/expect.poll instead of sleeps
Mock the network, not your own components
Keep e2e tests to critical paths

lessons.title: Web Performance & Core Web Vitals
lessons.summary_md: Core Web Vitals measure user experience: **LCP** (loading, under 2.5 s), **INP** (responsiveness, under 200 ms) and **CLS** (layout stability, under 0.1). Improve them by shipping less JavaScript, lazy-loading below-the-fold content, sizing images, and breaking up long tasks.
key_points: LCP: largest element painted; optimise hero images and fonts
INP: break up long tasks on the main thread
CLS: reserve space for images and ads
Measure field data, not just lab scores

lessons.title: Vue.js
lessons.summary_md: Vue components combine a template, script and styles. Vue 3 tracks dependencies with **Proxy-based reactivity**: `ref` and `reactive` values update the template automatically. The **Composition API** groups logic by feature; **Pinia** is the official store and **Nuxt** adds SSR.
key_points: ref() wraps primitives; access with .value in script
computed() caches derived values
v-for needs a :key
Pinia replaces Vuex

lessons.title: Angular
lessons.summary_md: Angular is a batteries-included framework built on TypeScript. It uses **dependency injection** for services, **RxJS observables** for async streams, and now **signals** for fine-grained change detection. Modules are giving way to standalone components.
key_points: Services are injected, not imported as singletons
Observables are lazy and can be cancelled
Signals avoid zone.js-wide change detection
Use the async pipe to subscribe in templates

lessons.title: Node.js
lessons.summary_md: Node.js runs JavaScript on the server with **non-blocking I/O**: the event loop hands slow work (disk, network) to libuv and continues serving requests. Never block it with heavy CPU work; use worker threads or a queue. Frameworks like Express/Fastify add routing and **middleware**.
key_points: One blocked event loop stalls every request
Middleware runs in order and can end the response
Streams process data without loading it all into memory
Handle errors in async routes or the process may crash

lessons.title: Python
lessons.summary_md: Python favours readable code. Know the core collections (**list, dict, set, tuple**), comprehensions, and functions with default and keyword arguments. Use **virtual environments** per project and `pip` to install packages. Beware mutable default arguments.
key_points: Lists are mutable, tuples are not
dicts preserve insertion order
Comprehensions build collections concisely
Never use a mutable object as a default argument

lessons.title: Python Web Frameworks
lessons.summary_md: **FastAPI** uses type hints and Pydantic models to validate requests and generate OpenAPI docs automatically. **Django** is a full framework with ORM, admin and auth. **Flask** is minimal. Pick FastAPI for async APIs, Django for content-heavy apps with an admin.
key_points: Pydantic validates and parses request bodies
Dependency injection in FastAPI shares DB sessions and auth
Django ships ORM, migrations and admin
Run async endpoints only with async drivers

lessons.title: REST API Design
lessons.summary_md: Good REST APIs model **resources** as nouns (`/users/42/orders`) and use HTTP methods for actions. Return precise status codes, paginate lists, validate every input, and make retries safe with **idempotency** (PUT and DELETE are idempotent; use idempotency keys for POST).
key_points: Nouns for resources, methods for verbs
201 Created for new resources, 204 for empty success
Cursor pagination is stable under inserts
Idempotency keys make POST retries safe

lessons.title: Authentication & Authorization
lessons.summary_md: **Authentication** answers who you are; **authorization** decides what you may do. Sessions store state server-side behind a cookie; **JWTs** are signed, self-contained tokens that cannot be revoked early without extra work. Use **OAuth 2.0 / OIDC** for "Sign in with..." and enforce permissions on the server, never only in the UI.
key_points: AuthN = identity, AuthZ = permissions
JWTs are signed, not encrypted
Short-lived access tokens plus refresh tokens
Check permissions server-side on every request

lessons.title: SQL
lessons.summary_md: SQL asks questions of tables. `SELECT` columns `FROM` a table, filter rows with `WHERE`, combine tables with **JOINs**, and summarise with `GROUP BY` plus aggregates (`COUNT`, `SUM`, `AVG`). `HAVING` filters groups after aggregation. NULL is not equal to anything, including NULL.
key_points: INNER JOIN keeps matches; LEFT JOIN keeps all left rows
WHERE filters rows, HAVING filters groups
Use IS NULL, never = NULL
Logical order: FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT, ORDER BY

lessons.title: Advanced SQL
lessons.summary_md: **CTEs** (`WITH ...`) name intermediate results and make long queries readable. **Window functions** (`ROW_NUMBER`, `RANK`, `LAG`, running `SUM`) compute across related rows without collapsing them like `GROUP BY` does. They are the core of analytics interviews.
key_points: Window functions keep every row
PARTITION BY restarts the window per group
ROW_NUMBER is unique, RANK leaves gaps, DENSE_RANK does not
LAG/LEAD compare a row with its neighbours

lessons.title: Relational Data Modeling
lessons.summary_md: Model entities as tables with a **primary key**, and relationships with **foreign keys** (a join table for many-to-many). **Normalise** to remove duplicated facts, then denormalise deliberately for read performance. Let the database enforce rules with NOT NULL, UNIQUE and CHECK constraints.
key_points: One fact in one place (normalisation)
Many-to-many needs a join table
Constraints are cheaper than application checks
Denormalise only with a measured reason

lessons.title: PostgreSQL & Relational Databases
lessons.summary_md: An **index** (usually a B-tree) turns a full table scan into a fast lookup, at the cost of slower writes. Read plans with `EXPLAIN ANALYZE`. **Transactions** group changes atomically; isolation levels control which concurrent changes you see. Connection pooling keeps databases healthy under load.
key_points: Index columns used in WHERE, JOIN and ORDER BY
ACID: atomic, consistent, isolated, durable
EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows the real plan and timings
Use a pooler (PgBouncer) for many short connections

lessons.title: NoSQL Databases
lessons.summary_md: NoSQL databases trade joins and flexible queries for scale or schema flexibility. **Document stores** (MongoDB) keep related data together; **key-value stores** (DynamoDB, Redis) are designed around known access patterns. Model data from the queries you need, not from entities.
key_points: Design around access patterns
Embed data read together; reference data shared widely
Partition keys decide scalability
Many NoSQL stores are eventually consistent by default

lessons.title: ORMs & Migrations
lessons.summary_md: ORMs like **Prisma**, **Drizzle** and **SQLAlchemy** map rows to typed objects and generate SQL. Watch for the **N+1 query** problem (one query per row in a loop) and fix it with joins or eager loading. Schema changes go through versioned **migrations** checked into git.
key_points: N+1 queries are the classic ORM performance bug
Migrations are versioned and reviewed like code
Make migrations backwards compatible for zero-downtime deploys
Drop to raw SQL for complex reports

lessons.title: Caching & Redis
lessons.summary_md: Caches trade freshness for speed. In **cache-aside**, the app reads the cache, falls back to the database on a miss and stores the result with a **TTL**. Invalidation is the hard part: delete or update keys when data changes. **Redis** also offers counters, sorted sets and locks.
key_points: Cache-aside: read cache, on miss read DB and populate
Every cached value needs a TTL or an invalidation path
LRU evicts the least recently used key
Beware the thundering herd when a hot key expires

lessons.title: Queues & Event Streaming
lessons.summary_md: Queues decouple producers from consumers so slow work happens in the background and spikes are absorbed. **RabbitMQ/SQS** deliver tasks to workers; **Kafka** keeps an ordered, replayable log per partition. Most systems give **at-least-once** delivery, so consumers must be **idempotent**.
key_points: At-least-once delivery means duplicates happen
Make consumers idempotent
Kafka orders messages within a partition only
Dead-letter queues capture poison messages

lessons.title: GraphQL
lessons.summary_md: GraphQL exposes a typed **schema**; clients ask for exactly the fields they need in one request. **Resolvers** fetch each field, which can cause N+1 queries; batch them with DataLoader. Mutations change data; subscriptions push updates.
key_points: One endpoint, client-shaped responses
Resolvers run per field
DataLoader batches and caches lookups
Limit query depth/complexity to prevent abuse

lessons.title: Microservices & gRPC
lessons.summary_md: Microservices split a system into independently deployable services around **business capabilities**. They talk over HTTP/**gRPC** or events. The cost is distributed failure: add **timeouts, retries with backoff and circuit breakers**, and trace requests across services. Start with a modular monolith.
key_points: Each service owns its data
Timeouts and retries with jitter on every remote call
Circuit breakers stop cascading failures
gRPC uses protobuf contracts and HTTP/2

lessons.title: Go (Golang)
lessons.summary_md: Go is a small, compiled language built for services. **Goroutines** are cheap concurrent functions and **channels** pass data between them. Errors are values you check explicitly. Use `context.Context` to cancel work and prevent goroutine leaks.
key_points: Goroutines are cheap; leaks are not
Do not communicate by sharing memory; share memory by communicating
Return errors, do not panic
Pass context for cancellation and deadlines

lessons.title: Java & Spring Boot
lessons.summary_md: Java is a statically typed JVM language used in large enterprises. **Spring Boot** wires applications through **dependency injection** and auto-configuration, exposing REST controllers and talking to databases through JPA/Hibernate. Java 21 **virtual threads** make blocking code scale.
key_points: Spring manages beans and injects dependencies
@RestController maps HTTP routes
JPA/Hibernate maps entities to tables
Virtual threads make thread-per-request cheap

lessons.title: Full Stack Architecture
lessons.summary_md: A full stack feature crosses the UI, an API and the database. Share **types and validation schemas** between client and server so contracts cannot drift, keep business logic on the server, and use **optimistic updates** for snappy UIs with rollback on failure.
key_points: One schema validates on both sides
Business rules live on the server
Optimistic UI needs a rollback path
Paginate and cache at the API boundary

lessons.title: Deploying Web Apps
lessons.summary_md: Managed platforms like Vercel, Netlify and Render deploy straight from git: every push builds, and pull requests get **preview environments**. Configure secrets as **environment variables**, never in the repo, and keep production, staging and preview separate.
key_points: Builds should be reproducible from a clean checkout
Secrets go in environment variables
Preview deployments per pull request
Roll back by redeploying the previous build

lessons.title: Linux Administration
lessons.summary_md: Most servers run Linux. Understand **users, groups and file permissions** (`chmod`, `chown`), manage **processes** (`ps`, `top`, `kill`) and **services** with systemd, read logs with `journalctl`, and install software with the package manager.
key_points: Permissions: read/write/execute for user, group, others
systemctl starts, stops and enables services
Everything is a file, including devices and sockets
Check disk, memory and load first when debugging

lessons.title: Shell Scripting
lessons.summary_md: Shell scripts glue tools together. Start scripts with `set -euo pipefail` so errors stop execution, **quote variables** to handle spaces, and use functions and exit codes. When logic grows beyond a page, switch to Python.
key_points: set -euo pipefail fails fast
Always quote "$variables"
$? holds the last exit code
Prefer Python for complex logic

lessons.title: Networking Fundamentals
lessons.summary_md: Packets travel by **IP address**; **TCP** adds reliable ordered delivery while **UDP** is fast and connectionless. **DNS** maps names to addresses. In the cloud you design **VPCs** with public and private **subnets** (CIDR ranges), route tables and security groups.
key_points: TCP is reliable and ordered; UDP is not
DNS resolves names; TTLs control caching
CIDR /24 = 256 addresses
Private subnets reach the internet via NAT

lessons.title: Docker & Containers
lessons.summary_md: A **container image** packages an app with its dependencies; a **container** is a running instance. Write Dockerfiles with **multi-stage builds** to keep images small, order layers so dependencies cache well, run as a **non-root** user, and use Compose for local multi-service setups.
key_points: Images are immutable layers; containers add a writable layer
Copy dependency manifests before source to use the layer cache
Multi-stage builds drop build tools from the final image
Run as non-root and pin base image versions

lessons.title: CI/CD Pipelines
lessons.summary_md: **Continuous integration** builds and tests every push; **continuous delivery** keeps main always deployable, and **continuous deployment** ships it automatically. Pipelines should be fast (cache dependencies, run jobs in parallel), reproducible, and keep secrets in the CI secret store.
key_points: CI runs on every push and pull request
Cache dependencies to keep pipelines fast
Build once, promote the same artifact through environments
Secrets come from the CI secret store

lessons.title: Kubernetes
lessons.summary_md: Kubernetes runs containers across a cluster and continuously reconciles the **desired state** you declare. **Pods** run containers, **Deployments** manage replicas and rolling updates, **Services** give stable networking, and **ConfigMaps/Secrets** inject configuration. Set resource requests/limits and health probes.
key_points: Declare desired state; controllers reconcile it
Deployments do rolling updates and rollbacks
Readiness probes gate traffic; liveness probes restart
Requests schedule pods, limits cap them

lessons.title: Cloud Platforms (AWS, GCP, Azure)
lessons.summary_md: Every cloud offers the same building blocks: **compute** (VMs, containers, functions), **storage** (object, block, managed databases), **networking** (VPCs, load balancers) and **identity** (IAM). Follow least privilege, spread across availability zones, and tag resources so you can track cost.
key_points: IAM: grant the least privilege needed
Use multiple availability zones for resilience
Object storage (S3) for files, managed DBs for data
Set budgets and alerts to avoid surprise bills

lessons.title: Infrastructure as Code
lessons.summary_md: Infrastructure as code makes environments reproducible and reviewable. **Terraform** compares your configuration with recorded **state** and shows a **plan** before applying. Store state remotely with locking, split code into modules, and never edit managed resources by hand.
key_points: plan before apply, every time
Remote state with locking for teams
Modules make infrastructure reusable
Manual changes cause drift

lessons.title: Monitoring & Observability
lessons.summary_md: Observability rests on three signals: **metrics** (cheap numbers over time), **logs** (detailed events) and **traces** (a request's path across services). Watch the four golden signals: latency, traffic, errors and saturation. Alert on user-facing symptoms, not every CPU spike.
key_points: Metrics, logs, traces
Golden signals: latency, traffic, errors, saturation
Structured logs are searchable
Alert on symptoms that need a human

lessons.title: SRE & Incident Response
lessons.summary_md: SRE turns reliability into numbers. An **SLI** measures something users feel (e.g. successful requests), an **SLO** sets the target (99.9%), and the **error budget** is the allowed failure that decides between shipping features and fixing reliability. Incidents end with a **blameless postmortem**.
key_points: SLI = measurement, SLO = target, SLA = contract
99.9% monthly allows about 43 minutes of downtime
Error budgets balance velocity and reliability
Postmortems fix systems, not people

lessons.title: GitOps (Argo CD)
lessons.summary_md: In GitOps the desired cluster state lives in a git repository, and an agent like **Argo CD** continuously syncs the cluster to it. Deployments become pull requests, rollbacks become reverts, and drift is detected automatically.
key_points: Git is the single source of truth
An in-cluster agent pulls changes
Rollback = git revert
Drift is detected and corrected

lessons.title: DevSecOps & Container Security
lessons.summary_md: DevSecOps builds security into the pipeline: **scan dependencies and images** (e.g. Trivy), run **SAST/DAST**, keep secrets in a manager, sign artifacts, and run containers with least privilege. Fail the build on critical findings.
key_points: Scan images and dependencies in CI
Secrets live in a secrets manager, not env files in git
Least privilege for workloads and pipelines
Sign and verify build artifacts

lessons.title: Web Servers & Reverse Proxies
lessons.summary_md: A **reverse proxy** like Nginx sits in front of app servers: it terminates **TLS**, serves static files, compresses responses and **load-balances** across instances. Learn server blocks, upstreams, and how proxy headers like `X-Forwarded-For` reach your app.
key_points: Reverse proxies face clients; apps stay private
Terminate TLS at the proxy
Round-robin and least-connections balancing
Forward client IP with X-Forwarded-For

lessons.title: Excel & Spreadsheets
lessons.summary_md: Spreadsheets are the analyst's first tool. Learn **relative vs absolute references** (`$A$1`), lookups (`XLOOKUP`/`VLOOKUP`), conditional aggregates (`SUMIFS`, `COUNTIFS`) and **pivot tables** for fast summaries. Keep raw data, calculations and outputs on separate sheets.
key_points: $ locks a row or column reference
XLOOKUP replaces VLOOKUP and INDEX/MATCH
Pivot tables summarise without formulas
Separate raw data from analysis

lessons.title: Statistics Fundamentals
lessons.summary_md: Statistics separates signal from noise. Describe data with **mean, median and spread**; reason about samples with the **central limit theorem**; test hypotheses with **p-values** and report **confidence intervals**. Correlation does not imply causation, and the median resists outliers.
key_points: Median is robust to outliers; mean is not
A p-value is P(data this extreme | null is true)
Confidence intervals show the plausible range
Correlation is not causation

lessons.title: Data Cleaning & Wrangling
lessons.summary_md: Real data is messy, and cleaning is most of an analyst's job. Profile first (row counts, nulls, distinct values), then fix **types**, standardise **formats**, remove **duplicates**, and decide explicitly how to treat **missing values** and outliers. Document every rule so results are reproducible.
key_points: Profile before you clean
Decide on missing values: drop, impute or flag
Deduplicate on a clear key
Keep cleaning steps scripted and reproducible

lessons.title: NumPy
lessons.summary_md: NumPy's **ndarray** stores numbers in contiguous memory so operations run in fast C loops. Replace Python loops with **vectorised** expressions, understand **broadcasting** rules for combining shapes, and use boolean masks for filtering.
key_points: Vectorise instead of looping
Broadcasting aligns shapes from the right
Boolean masks filter arrays
Check .shape and .dtype constantly

lessons.title: pandas for Data Analysis
lessons.summary_md: pandas brings SQL-like operations to Python. A **DataFrame** is a table of typed columns. Filter with boolean masks, `groupby().agg()` to summarise, `merge` to join, and `pivot_table` to reshape. Avoid row-by-row `apply` when a vectorised method exists.
key_points: groupby + agg = SQL GROUP BY
merge = SQL JOIN
Use .loc for label-based selection
Vectorised ops beat apply

lessons.title: Data Visualization
lessons.summary_md: Pick the chart for the question: **bar** to compare categories, **line** for change over time, **scatter** for relationships, **histogram** for distributions. Start bar axes at zero, remove chart junk, label directly, and use colour to highlight, not decorate.
key_points: Bar = compare, line = trend, scatter = relationship
Bar charts start at zero
Highlight the one thing that matters
Avoid pie charts with many slices

lessons.title: BI Tools (Tableau, Power BI)
lessons.summary_md: BI tools connect to data sources and let you build **interactive dashboards**. Model data cleanly first (one fact table, dimension tables), define **measures** once (DAX in Power BI, calculated fields in Tableau), and design dashboards around the decisions their users make.
key_points: Clean model first, visuals second
Define metrics once and reuse them
Filters and drill-downs replace many static charts
Every dashboard answers a named question

lessons.title: Analytics Engineering (dbt)
lessons.summary_md: **dbt** turns SQL `SELECT`s into versioned, tested models in the warehouse (Snowflake, BigQuery). Layer models from staging to marts, use a **star schema** (facts and dimensions) for reporting, and add tests for uniqueness and not-null keys.
key_points: Staging, intermediate, marts
Facts hold events, dimensions describe them
Test keys for unique and not_null
Docs and lineage come from the code

lessons.title: Data Storytelling
lessons.summary_md: Analysis only matters if it changes a decision. Lead with the **answer and recommendation**, support it with two or three charts, quantify impact, and state caveats plainly. Tailor depth to the audience: executives want the "so what", analysts want the method.
key_points: Answer first, then evidence
One message per chart
Quantify the impact of the recommendation
State assumptions and limitations

lessons.title: A/B Testing & Experimentation
lessons.summary_md: An A/B test randomly splits users to measure a change's causal effect. Define one **primary metric** and guardrails up front, compute the **sample size** from the minimum detectable effect, run for full weeks, and do not stop early when the result looks significant ("peeking").
key_points: Randomise at the unit you analyse
Pick the primary metric before launch
Sample size depends on baseline and minimum detectable effect
Peeking inflates false positives

lessons.title: Product Analytics
lessons.summary_md: Product analytics explains how users move through a product. **Funnels** show where users drop off, **cohorts** show whether retention improves over time, and a **North Star metric** captures the value users get. Instrument events with consistent names and properties.
key_points: Funnels locate drop-off
Cohort retention curves should flatten, not hit zero
North Star = delivered user value, with input metrics beneath it
Consistent event naming makes analysis possible

lessons.title: Math for Machine Learning
lessons.summary_md: ML models are functions of **vectors and matrices** trained by **gradient descent**: compute the derivative of the loss with respect to each parameter and step against it. Know matrix multiplication shapes, the dot product as similarity, and how the learning rate affects convergence.
key_points: (m x n) times (n x p) gives (m x p)
The gradient points uphill; step the other way
Too high a learning rate diverges, too low crawls
Dot product measures alignment of vectors

lessons.title: Machine Learning Fundamentals
lessons.summary_md: Supervised learning fits a model from labelled examples. Split data into **train/validation/test**, start with a simple baseline, and watch for **overfitting** (great training score, poor validation). Choose metrics that match the problem: precision/recall for imbalanced classes, RMSE for regression. Never let test data leak into training.
key_points: Train, validate, then test once
Overfitting: low training error, high validation error
Accuracy misleads on imbalanced data
Data leakage makes results look better than reality

lessons.title: Deep Learning (PyTorch)
lessons.summary_md: Neural networks stack layers of linear transforms and non-linear activations, trained by **backpropagation**. A PyTorch training loop is: forward pass, compute loss, `loss.backward()`, `optimizer.step()`, `optimizer.zero_grad()`. Use GPUs, mini-batches, and regularisation (dropout, weight decay) to train well.
key_points: Forward, loss, backward, step, zero_grad
Activations add non-linearity
Batch size and learning rate interact
Dropout and weight decay fight overfitting

lessons.title: NLP & Transformers
lessons.summary_md: Transformers process text as **tokens** mapped to **embeddings** and use **self-attention** to let every token weigh every other token. Encoder models (BERT) suit classification and embeddings; decoder models (GPT) generate text. Hugging Face provides pretrained models to fine-tune.
key_points: Text becomes tokens, tokens become vectors
Self-attention relates every token to every other
Encoders understand, decoders generate
Fine-tune pretrained models instead of training from scratch

lessons.title: LLM Apps & Prompt Engineering
lessons.summary_md: LLM features are built from **prompts, tools and evaluation**. Give clear instructions and examples, request **structured output** and validate it, let the model call **tools** for facts it cannot know, and build an **eval set** before tuning prompts. Never trust model output for URLs, numbers or security decisions without checking.
key_points: Validate structured output with a schema
Tools/function calling ground the model in real data
Build evals before iterating on prompts
Models hallucinate; verify facts and links

lessons.title: RAG & Vector Search
lessons.summary_md: Retrieval-augmented generation answers questions from your own data: **chunk** documents, **embed** each chunk, store vectors in a **vector database**, retrieve the nearest chunks for a query (often combined with keyword search), and pass them to the model with instructions to cite them. Measure retrieval quality separately from answer quality.
key_points: Chunk size trades context for precision
Cosine similarity ranks nearest chunks
Hybrid search mixes keywords and vectors
Evaluate retrieval (recall@k) and answers separately

lessons.title: MLOps & Model Deployment
lessons.summary_md: MLOps applies DevOps to models. **Track experiments** (parameters, data versions, metrics), package models in containers, serve them behind an API, and **monitor** for data drift and performance decay. Reproducibility needs versioned data, code and environment.
key_points: Version data, code and model together
Track every experiment
Monitor input drift and prediction quality
Retrain on a schedule or on drift alerts

lessons.title: Data Pipelines (Spark, Airflow)
lessons.summary_md: Data pipelines move and transform data on a schedule. **Spark** distributes transformations across a cluster using lazy DataFrames; **Airflow** orchestrates tasks as DAGs with retries and backfills. Make tasks **idempotent** so reruns are safe, and partition data by date.
key_points: Spark is lazy until an action runs
Airflow DAGs define dependencies and schedules
Idempotent tasks make backfills safe
Partition by date for efficient reads

lessons.title: Computer Vision
lessons.summary_md: Computer vision models learn features from pixels. **CNNs** use convolutions to detect local patterns; vision transformers split images into patches. Tasks range from classification to **object detection** (boxes, e.g. YOLO) and **segmentation** (pixel masks). Augmentation and transfer learning matter more than architecture for small datasets.
key_points: Convolutions share weights across the image
Detection predicts boxes; segmentation predicts masks
Transfer learning beats training from scratch on small data
Augment data to improve robustness

lessons.title: Fine-Tuning LLMs
lessons.summary_md: Fine-tune only when prompting and retrieval are not enough. **LoRA** trains small low-rank adapter matrices instead of all weights; **QLoRA** does it on a quantised model to fit consumer GPUs. Quality depends mostly on clean, representative training data and a held-out evaluation set.
key_points: Try prompting and RAG first
LoRA trains small adapters, not all weights
QLoRA quantises the base model to save memory
Data quality beats data quantity

lessons.title: User Research & Discovery
lessons.summary_md: Discovery reduces the risk of building the wrong thing. Interview users about **past behaviour, not hypothetical futures** (The Mom Test), look for repeated pain, and synthesise findings into problems, **jobs to be done** and personas. Separate the problem from your favourite solution.
key_points: Ask about what people did, not what they would do
Compliments are not evidence
Synthesize patterns across 5+ interviews
Frame the problem before proposing solutions

lessons.title: Market Sizing & Competitive Analysis
lessons.summary_md: **TAM** is the whole market, **SAM** the part your product can serve, and **SOM** what you can realistically win. Size bottom-up (customers x price) rather than quoting top-down reports. Map competitors on the dimensions customers care about and identify what makes your position defensible.
key_points: TAM > SAM > SOM
Bottom-up sizing is more credible
Compare competitors on customer-valued dimensions
Moats: network effects, switching costs, data, brand

lessons.title: PRDs & User Stories
lessons.summary_md: A PRD aligns the team on **why** and **what**, leaving **how** to engineering and design. Include the problem, target users, goals and success metrics, scope and non-goals, user stories ("As a..., I want..., so that...") with **acceptance criteria**, edge cases and open questions.
key_points: Problem and success metric come first
Non-goals prevent scope creep
Acceptance criteria are testable
List open questions and risks

lessons.title: Prioritization Frameworks
lessons.summary_md: **RICE** scores ideas by Reach x Impact x Confidence / Effort. **MoSCoW** buckets scope into Must, Should, Could and Won't. Frameworks make trade-offs explicit and comparable, but they inform judgment rather than replace it; revisit scores as evidence changes.
key_points: RICE = Reach x Impact x Confidence / Effort
MoSCoW: Must, Should, Could, Won't
Confidence penalises guesses
Frameworks support judgment, they do not replace it

lessons.title: Agile, Scrum & Delivery
lessons.summary_md: Agile teams deliver in small increments and adjust from feedback. **Scrum** uses fixed sprints with planning, daily stand-ups, review and retrospective; **Kanban** limits work in progress on a continuous flow. Keep the backlog refined and stories small enough to finish in a few days.
key_points: Small batches give faster feedback
Scrum ceremonies: planning, daily, review, retro
Kanban limits work in progress
A story is done when it meets the definition of done

lessons.title: Product Strategy & Roadmapping
lessons.summary_md: Strategy is a set of choices about **where to play and how to win**. Translate the vision into a few measurable goals (OKRs), then a **roadmap of outcomes**, not a list of features with dates. Communicate what you are not doing as clearly as what you are.
key_points: Strategy is choosing what not to do
Roadmaps should show outcomes and problems
OKRs: an objective plus measurable key results
Revisit strategy when evidence changes

lessons.title: Stakeholder Management
lessons.summary_md: Influence without authority starts with understanding what each stakeholder needs. Map stakeholders by influence and interest, share context early, write decisions down with their rationale, and **disagree and commit** once a decision is made. Surprises erode trust faster than bad news.
key_points: Map stakeholders by influence and interest
Share bad news early
Write decisions and rationale down
Disagree, then commit

lessons.title: Product Sense
lessons.summary_md: Product sense interviews test structured creativity. Clarify the goal, pick a **user segment**, list their **pain points**, prioritise one, brainstorm solutions, choose with explicit trade-offs, and define **success metrics** and risks. Show your reasoning out loud.
key_points: Goal, users, pains, solutions, metrics
Pick one segment and go deep
Prioritise pains by frequency and severity
End with metrics and risks

lessons.title: Visual Hierarchy & Design Principles
lessons.summary_md: Good interfaces guide the eye. Build **hierarchy** with size, weight and colour so the most important element wins; group related items by **proximity**; **align** everything to a shared edge; and use generous **whitespace**. Consistency lets users predict how things work.
key_points: Hierarchy: one clear primary element per view
Proximity groups related items
Alignment creates order
Whitespace is a feature, not wasted space

lessons.title: Typography
lessons.summary_md: Most interfaces are text. Use a **type scale** (e.g. ratio 1.25) for consistent sizes, keep body text at 16px or more with line height around 1.5, limit line length to about 45-75 characters, and stick to one or two typefaces with clear weight contrast.
key_points: Use a modular type scale
Body text 16px+, line height ~1.5
45-75 characters per line
One or two typefaces are enough

lessons.title: Color & Contrast
lessons.summary_md: Define colours by **role** (primary, surface, text, success, danger) rather than by hue, with a range of shades for each. Check **contrast** (4.5:1 for body text) and never use colour as the only signal; pair it with icons or text. Design light and dark themes from the same tokens.
key_points: Name colours by role, not hue
Body text contrast at least 4.5:1
Never rely on colour alone
Shades give depth without new hues

lessons.title: Layout Grids & Spacing
lessons.summary_md: Grids make layouts consistent and responsive. Use a **column grid** (12 columns on desktop, 4 on mobile) with consistent gutters, and a **spacing scale** based on 8 (4, 8, 16, 24, 32...). When every gap comes from the scale, screens feel coherent.
key_points: 12 columns desktop, 4 on mobile
Spacing from a scale of 4/8
Gutters stay consistent
Align content to columns, not arbitrary positions

lessons.title: Figma Fundamentals
lessons.summary_md: Figma is the industry-standard design tool. Work in **frames** (screens), organise **layers** with clear names, define reusable **styles** for colour and text, and collaborate through comments and shared libraries. Learn keyboard shortcuts early.
key_points: Frames are screens or containers
Name layers for handoff
Styles keep colour and type consistent
Comment and share instead of exporting

lessons.title: Figma Auto Layout & Components
lessons.summary_md: **Auto Layout** makes frames behave like Flexbox: direction, spacing, padding and resizing (hug, fill, fixed). **Components** with **variants** and properties (boolean, text, instance swap) let one master drive every instance, so updates propagate everywhere.
key_points: Auto Layout = Flexbox for designers
Hug contents vs fill container
Variants model states like hover and disabled
Edit the main component, not instances

lessons.title: Design Systems & Tokens
lessons.summary_md: A design system is the shared language between design and engineering: **tokens** (colour, type, spacing, radius), **components** with documented states, and usage guidelines. Name tokens by purpose (`color.text.muted`), version the system, and keep Figma and code in sync.
key_points: Tokens: the smallest named design decisions
Document states and usage for every component
Purpose-based names survive rebrands
Version and communicate changes

lessons.title: Wireframing & User Flows
lessons.summary_md: **User flows** map the steps a user takes to reach a goal; **wireframes** sketch the structure of each screen without visual polish. Staying low-fidelity keeps feedback focused on structure and makes throwing ideas away cheap.
key_points: Flow first, screens second
Low fidelity invites honest feedback
Include empty, error and loading states
Annotate intent for engineers

lessons.title: Interactive Prototyping
lessons.summary_md: Prototypes let you test an experience before anyone writes code. Link frames with interactions, use smart animate for transitions, and build only the paths you need to test. Match fidelity to the question: low for flow, high for visual and interaction details.
key_points: Prototype the path you are testing
Fidelity matches the question
Smart animate for transitions
Prototypes are disposable

lessons.title: Interaction Design
lessons.summary_md: Interaction design shapes how a product responds. Every action needs **feedback** within about 100 ms, controls need clear **affordances**, and every component needs designed states (default, hover, focus, active, disabled, loading, error). Motion should explain change, not decorate; respect reduced-motion settings.
key_points: Feedback within ~100 ms feels instant
Design every state, including errors
Motion explains spatial change
Respect prefers-reduced-motion

lessons.title: Usability Testing
lessons.summary_md: Give 5 representative users realistic **tasks**, ask them to **think aloud**, and observe without helping. Note where they hesitate or fail, rate severity, and fix the worst issues first. A quick **heuristic evaluation** (e.g. Nielsen's 10) catches obvious problems before testing.
key_points: Five users find most major issues
Give tasks, not instructions
Do not lead or help
Prioritise by severity and frequency

lessons.title: Information Architecture
lessons.summary_md: Information architecture decides how content is grouped, labelled and navigated. Use **card sorting** to learn users' mental models, a **sitemap** to define structure, and **tree testing** to check people can find things. Label in users' words, not internal jargon.
key_points: Card sorting reveals mental models
Tree testing validates navigation
Use users' vocabulary for labels
Shallow, clear hierarchies beat deep ones

lessons.title: UX Writing & Microcopy
lessons.summary_md: Words are interface. Write **buttons as verbs** that describe the outcome ("Save changes"), **errors** that say what happened and how to fix it, and **empty states** that suggest the next step. Be concise, consistent and human.
key_points: Buttons describe the action's result
Errors explain the problem and the fix
Empty states suggest a next step
Use the same word for the same thing everywhere

lessons.title: Design Portfolio & Case Studies
lessons.summary_md: Hiring managers skim. Show **2-3 deep case studies** rather than many shallow ones. Each should state the problem, your role, constraints, the process (research, iterations, trade-offs), the final design and the **measured outcome**. Show messy middle steps; they prove your thinking.
key_points: Quality over quantity: 2-3 case studies
State your role and constraints
Show iterations and trade-offs
End with outcomes and learnings

lessons.title: Object-Oriented Programming
lessons.summary_md: Object-oriented programming models a program as objects that hold data and behaviour. The four pillars are encapsulation (hide state behind methods), abstraction (expose what, not how), inheritance (reuse and specialise) and polymorphism (one interface, many implementations). Campus interviews ask you to define each with an example, compare abstract classes and interfaces, and design small systems such as a parking lot.
key_points: Explain each pillar with a short code example.
Prefer composition over inheritance when behaviour varies.
SOLID keeps classes small and easy to change.

lessons.title: Operating Systems
lessons.summary_md: An operating system shares the CPU, memory and devices between programs. Interviews focus on processes versus threads, scheduling algorithms, race conditions and locks, the four conditions for deadlock, and virtual memory with paging. Be ready to compute waiting times for a small scheduling example and to explain what happens on a page fault.
key_points: A process has its own address space; threads share one.
Deadlock needs mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption and circular wait.
Paging maps virtual pages to physical frames.

lessons.title: Computer Networks
lessons.summary_md: Computer networks move data in layers: application (HTTP, DNS), transport (TCP, UDP), network (IP) and link. Interviews ask what happens when you type a URL, how TCP makes delivery reliable, the difference between TCP and UDP, how DNS resolves a name, and how HTTPS protects traffic with TLS.
key_points: TCP is reliable and ordered; UDP is fast and connectionless.
DNS turns a name into an IP address through a chain of servers.
HTTPS is HTTP over TLS.

lessons.title: Database Management Systems
lessons.summary_md: A DBMS stores data safely and answers queries. Interviews cover keys (primary, foreign, candidate), normal forms up to BCNF, joins and aggregation in SQL, ACID transactions, isolation levels and their anomalies, and how B-tree indexes speed up lookups. Expect to write two or three SQL queries live.
key_points: Normalise to remove update anomalies; denormalise for read speed.
ACID: atomicity, consistency, isolation, durability.
An index trades write cost and space for faster reads.

lessons.title: Quantitative Aptitude
lessons.summary_md: Quantitative aptitude sections in campus tests (TCS NQT, Infosys, Wipro, Accenture, Cognizant, Capgemini) reward speed with a small set of formulas. Learn the shortcut for each topic, practise under a timer, and skip a question that takes more than two minutes.
key_points: Convert percentages to fractions (12.5% = 1/8) to calculate faster.
Time and work: add rates, not times.
Check the answer options before solving fully.

lessons.title: Logical Reasoning
lessons.summary_md: Logical reasoning tests pattern spotting and careful reading. Draw diagrams for blood relations, directions and seating; write the rules of a code before decoding; and for syllogisms use Venn diagrams rather than intuition.
key_points: Draw, do not imagine: a quick diagram prevents most errors.
Number series: check differences, then ratios, then alternating patterns.
Syllogisms: a conclusion must hold in every possible diagram.

lessons.title: Verbal Ability
lessons.summary_md: Verbal sections check reading speed and grammar. Read the questions before the passage, answer from the text rather than opinion, and learn the common error types: subject-verb agreement, tense, articles, prepositions and parallel structure.
key_points: Answer from the passage, not from what you already know.
Para-jumbles: find the opening sentence and linked pairs first.
Most correction questions test agreement, tense or prepositions.
